content: 1. Drug Interactions with Ethinyl Estradiol: BCRP Substrates: Inhibitors of BCRP may increase the effects and toxicity of BCRP substrates. It is recommended to use the lowest starting dose of the BCRP substrate or consider reducing its dose. Oxcarbazepine: This drug decreases the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Hormonal contraceptive efficacy may be reduced; nonhormonal contraceptives are advised. Paromomycin, Penicillin G, Penicillin VK: These antibiotics may reduce ethinyl estradiol levels by altering intestinal flora, potentially lowering contraceptive efficacy. Monitor closely, though the risk of contraceptive failure is low. Phenobarbital, Phenytoin, Primidone: These drugs reduce ethinyl estradiol levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Hormonal contraceptive efficacy may be compromised; nonhormonal contraceptives are recommended. Pioglitazone: This drug decreases ethinyl estradiol levels through an unknown mechanism. Caution and monitoring are advised. Posaconazole, Quinidine, Quinupristin/Dalfopristin: These drugs increase ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 or P-glycoprotein metabolism. Monitor closely for potential adverse effects. Ramelteon: Ethinyl estradiol increases ramelteon levels by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. Monitor for potential side effects. Ranolazine: Ethinyl estradiol increases ranolazine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid or use alternative drugs. Rifampin, Rifabutin, Rifapentine: These drugs decrease ethinyl estradiol levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism, reducing contraceptive efficacy. Nonhormonal contraceptives are recommended. St. John’s Wort: This herbal supplement reduces ethinyl estradiol levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism, potentially reducing contraceptive efficacy. Avoid or use alternative methods. Sugammadex: Additional nonhormonal contraceptive methods are required for seven days after administration. Tetracyclines, Sulfonamides (e.g., Sulfamethoxazole): These antibiotics may reduce ethinyl estradiol levels by altering intestinal flora. The risk of contraceptive failure is low, but caution is advised. Topiramate: This drug reduces ethinyl estradiol levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Nonhormonal contraceptives are recommended. Tucatinib: This drug increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid coadministration or adjust doses as needed. Valproic Acid: Ethinyl estradiol increases valproic acid elimination, potentially leading to increased seizure frequency. Monitor closely. Voriconazole: This drug increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor for adverse effects. 2. Adverse Effects of Ethinyl Estradiol: Common side effects include headache, emotional lability, breast symptoms, menstrual cramps, abdominal pain, nausea, and application site reactions. Serious risks include arterial or venous thromboembolism, hypertension, myocardial infarction, cerebral hemorrhage, gallbladder disease, and hepatic adenomas. Contraindications include active or history of breast cancer, arterial thromboembolic disease (e.g., stroke, myocardial infarction), thrombotic disorders (e.g., DVT/PE), estrogen-dependent neoplasia, liver disease, and uncontrolled hypertension. 3. Special Considerations: Avoid use in women with additional risk factors for thromboembolism postpartum. Wait at least three weeks after vaginal delivery or six weeks after cesarean section before initiating combined hormonal contraceptives. Ethinyl estradiol may reduce the quality and quantity of breast milk. Alternative birth control methods are recommended until full weaning. 4. Cancer Risks: Some studies suggest an increased risk of breast cancer with oral contraceptive use, while others do not. Risk factors include early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, and first childbirth after age 30. Long-term use of oral contraceptives (five or more years) may increase the risk of cervical and liver cancer. 5. Pharmacokinetics: Ethinyl estradiol has a half-life of 28 hours and is extensively bound to serum albumin. It undergoes hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4 and is excreted in urine and bile, undergoing enterohepatic recycling. 6. Pregnancy and Lactation: Ethinyl estradiol is contraindicated during pregnancy (Category X). Small amounts are excreted in breast milk, and estrogens may reduce milk production. 7. Mechanism of Action: Ethinyl estradiol suppresses gonadotropin release, preventing ovulation. It also increases DNA, RNA, and protein synthesis in target tissues. 8. Monitoring and Adjustments: Monitor for drug interactions, especially with CYP3A4 substrates or inhibitors. Adjust dosages as clinically indicated to avoid reduced efficacy or increased toxicity.
